```{r setup-time, include=FALSE}
library(here)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, dpi = 110)
source(here("analysis", "reports", "descriptive_plots", "R", "time_analysis.R"))
```

```{=html}
<hr>
<h1 id="time">How long the survey takes, and why that varies</h1>

<div class="block-box">
<strong>A question about the instrument, not the respondents.</strong> Completion
times differ several-fold. This tab asks what that says about how the survey
works - where it asks too much, whether speed costs data quality, and what to
expect when it runs for real. Nothing here is about drug policy.
<br><br>
<strong>No time is capped, trimmed or winsorised.</strong> Someone who took half
an hour took half an hour: that is the phenomenon, not an outlier to be tidied
away. Where the spread makes a figure unreadable the <em>axis</em> is logged,
which compresses the scale without dropping a single respondent.
<br><br>
<strong>What this data cannot show.</strong> The panel agency exported one
number, <code>InterviewDuration</code> in seconds, and no per-page timings. So "which page is slow?" is unanswerable here, and everything below
infers from total duration crossed with what people answered. Section E says
what follows from that.
</div>
```

## A. The distribution

```{r time-distribution}
# Quantiles rather than a mean and SD: the distribution is right-skewed, so the
# mean sits above the typical respondent and the SD implies a symmetry it does
# not have.
duration <- pilot$duration_min
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    statistiek = c("minimum", "5e percentiel", "1e kwartiel", "mediaan",
                   "3e kwartiel", "90e percentiel", "95e percentiel", "maximum"),
    minuten = round(c(min(duration),
                      quantile(duration, c(.05, .25, .5, .75, .90, .95)),
                      max(duration)), 1),
    row.names = NULL),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0("Completion time, all ", length(duration),
                   " respondents - none excluded."))
```

```{r time-histogram, fig.height=3.4}
# Log x-axis: the tail is long enough that a linear axis puts nine tenths of the
# sample in the leftmost two bars. Every respondent is still plotted.
breaks <- c(2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 35)
ggplot(data.frame(duration), aes(x = duration)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#3B6EA5", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(duration), colour = "#B2182B", linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = breaks, labels = breaks) +
  labs(title = "Completion time (log scale)",
       subtitle = paste0("dashed line = median, ", round(median(duration), 1),
                         " minutes; nothing capped"),
       x = "minuten", y = "respondenten") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9))
```

```{r time-extremes, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf(paste("The slowest respondent took %.1f minutes and the fastest",
                  "%.1f - a factor of %.1f. %d finished in under five minutes;",
                  "%d took more than twenty.\n\n"),
            max(duration), min(duration), max(duration) / min(duration),
            sum(duration < 5), sum(duration > 20)))
```

## B. Response patterns against time

The question this tab was asked: do the people who finish quickly answer
differently? Each measure below targets one way of getting through a survey
without reading it. They are defined in `R/time_analysis.R`, and each is a count
or a proportion that can be checked by hand.

```{r time-patterns}
patterns <- response_patterns(pilot, likert_cols, slider_cols,
                              SCALE_MIN, SCALE_MAX)
# `slider_default` counts sliders left at 50, the position a Qualtrics slider
# starts at. The agency stored a chosen rule, and 50 is rule 5 (alleen in
# speciaalzaak, zonder winst) - an answer, not an untouched slider.
patterns$slider_default <- NULL
knitr::kable(correlate_with_duration(patterns, duration), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste("Each response-pattern measure against log",
                             "completion time (Spearman, with a 95% interval)."))
```

**Read the interval, not the correlation.** A coefficient near zero means one of
two quite different things: the effect is absent, or the sample is too small to
see it. The interval separates those, and an interval that spans zero widely
supports neither conclusion.

```{r time-patterns-plot, fig.height=3.6}
# The two measures most often used to catch careless responding, plotted against
# time so the shape of the (non-)relationship is visible rather than summarised.
plot_data <- data.frame(
  duration = rep(duration, 2),
  waarde   = c(patterns$sd_likert, patterns$longest_run),
  maat     = rep(c("spreiding in antwoorden (SD)",
                   "langste reeks gelijke antwoorden"), each = nrow(patterns)))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = duration, y = waarde)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#3B6EA5", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
              colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ maat, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "minuten (log)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9))
```

## C. Does speed cost data quality?

Section B cannot answer this. A measure can be uncorrelated with duration while
the fast group still produces a less coherent scale — the correlations look at
respondents one at a time, and reliability is a property of the group.

```{r time-quality}
# Equal-sized speed groups, and the reliability of the belief scale within each.
knitr::kable(quality_by_speed(scored_items, duration), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste("Scale quality by speed group. alpha is Cronbach's",
                             "alpha over the scored items; item-rest is the mean",
                             "corrected item-total correlation."))
```

```{r time-quality-note, results='asis'}
q <- quality_by_speed(scored_items, duration)
cat(sprintf(paste("Alpha runs %s from the fastest group to the slowest",
                  "(%s). With about %d respondents per group this is a",
                  "difference to note rather than to rely on.\n\n"),
            # compared at the two decimals that are printed
            switch(sign(round(q$alpha[nrow(q)], 2) - round(q$alpha[1], 2)) + 2,
                   "**down**", "**flat**", "**up**"),
            paste(sprintf("%.2f", q$alpha), collapse = " / "),
            round(mean(q$n))))
```

## D. Who takes longer

```{r time-groups}
# Median duration per group, always with the cell size beside it. The soft
# launch's own groupings: the agency's recodes (raw codes where the export
# carries no labels) and the substance ladder. There is no survey language.
groupings <- list(
  list(pilot$leeftijd,          "leeftijd"),
  list(pilot$substance_ladder,  "middelengebruik"),
  list(pilot$opleiding,         "opleiding (edu_3_rec)"),
  list(pilot$stemherinnering,   "stemherinnering (vote_recall_rec)"),
  list(pilot$geslacht,          "geslacht (sex_rec)"),
  list(pilot$stedelijkheid,     "stedelijkheid (urb)")
)
knitr::kable(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(groupings, function(g)
    duration_by_group(duration, g[[1]], g[[2]]))),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Median completion time per group, in minutes, with cell sizes.")
```

**Why every row carries an `n`.** A median resting on one or two respondents
can look like a large difference. A table of medians without cell sizes would
present that as a finding; no row whose `n` is small is one.

```{r time-age, fig.height=3.4}
# Age is the clearest relationship here, so it gets the plot.
ggplot(data.frame(age = pilot$leeftijd, duration),
       aes(x = age, y = duration)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#eef2f6", colour = "grey40", outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.18, height = 0, colour = "#3B6EA5", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(10)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "minuten (log)",
       title = "Completion time by age band",
       subtitle = "every respondent shown; the axis is logged, nothing is capped") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9))
```

## E. What this data cannot say

- **Which page is slow.** There are no per-page timings. A question that takes
  four minutes and one that takes ten seconds are indistinguishable in a single
  total.
- **Slow reading from a slow lunch.** `Duration` is wall-clock time from first
  to last click. A respondent who left the tab open for a coffee is recorded the
  same as one who read every item twice.
- What *can* be checked is whether the slow tail looks careless, which is what
  sections B and C show.

## F. Who did not finish

```{r time-dropouts}
# Attrition: the interviews the agency marks InProgress. `dropped` comes from
# the data layer. The export has no progress percentage and no duration for an
# unfinished interview, so how far each one got is read off the answers: the
# last block, in questionnaire order, with at least one item answered.
if (nrow(dropped) == 0) {
  cat("Every interview was completed: no attrition to report.\n")
} else {
  survey_blocks <- list(beleidsvoorkeur = slider_cols,
                        opvattingen     = select_items("beliefs", names(dropped)),
                        gedrag          = select_items("gedrag_beleid", names(dropped)),
                        middelengebruik = subst_cols,
                        emoties         = emotion_cols,
                        betrokkenheid   = invol_cols)
  reached <- sapply(survey_blocks, function(cols) rowSums(!is.na(dropped[cols])) > 0)
  last <- apply(reached, 1, function(r)
    if (any(r)) names(survey_blocks)[max(which(r))] else "geen enkel blok")
  knitr::kable(
    as.data.frame(table(`laatste blok beantwoord` =
                          factor(last, c("geen enkel blok", names(survey_blocks)))),
                  responseName = "interviews"),
    row.names = FALSE,
    caption = paste0(nrow(dropped), " of ", n_genuine,
                     " interviews were not completed and are not analysed."))
}
```

## G. What to change for the main study

```{r time-recommendations, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "- **Add a Timing question to each page.** It is the one change that would ",
  "turn the unanswerable question in section E into a direct measurement, and ",
  "it costs respondents nothing.\n",
  "- **Quote about %d minutes** to participants: the median here is %.1f and ",
  "three quarters finish within %.1f.\n",
  "- **Budget for the tail.** The slowest respondent needed %.1f minutes; a ",
  "reward calculated on the median underpays the slowest quarter.\n"),
  round(median(duration)), median(duration),
  quantile(duration, .75), max(duration)))

fast <- sum(duration < 5)
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "- **A speed-based exclusion rule** needs a reason in sections B and C. %d ",
  "respondents finished in under five minutes.\n"), fast))
```
